title: Nationalism and Nation - Building in Postcolonial Contexts
sources_used: V Semester MGU UGP (Honours) - 2024 Admission regular Examination October 2026

questions.question: Give one criticism of the primordialist view of nationalism. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Primordialists (Edward Shils, 1957; Clifford Geertz, 1963) treat national attachments as
  • natural, ancient and fixed 'givens' of blood, language, religion and territory - main
  • criticism: the view cannot explain why nations emerge only at particular historical
  • moments, or why identities change, merge or disappear- modernists (Gellner, Hobsbawm,
  • Anderson) show nations to be recent products of industrialisation, print and the modern
  • state- Eller and Coughlan (1993) call primordial ties asserted rather than explained -
  • ignores the 'invention of tradition' (Hobsbawm and Ranger, 1983) and elite manipulation
  • of identity (Paul Brass's instrumentalism). [Any one criticism]
questions.source_exam: V Semester MGU UGP (Honours) - 2024 Admission regular Examination October 2026

questions.question: Give one reason why nationalism became strong during the colonial period. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Shared experience of colonial domination created a common enemy and common
  • grievances- economic exploitation (Dadabhai Naoroji's 'drain of wealth') - racial
  • discrimination and exclusion of the colonised from higher administration - Western
  • education, print, railways and a unified colonial administration produced a connected
  • middle class familiar with ideas of liberty and self-determination- cultural assertion in the
  • 'inner domain' (Partha Chatterjee). [Any one reason]
questions.source_exam: V Semester MGU UGP (Honours) - 2024 Admission regular Examination October 2026

questions.question: How did Indonesia's 1945 declaration of independence lead to further conflict? / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Sukarno and Hatta proclaimed independence on 17 August 1945, two days after Japan's
  • surrender- the Netherlands refused to recognise the Republic a nd returned behind Allied
  • (British) forces to restore colonial rule - led to the Indonesian National Revolution (1945 -
  • 49): Battle of Surabaya (October -December 1945), the Linggadjati (1946 -47) and
  • Renville (1948) agreements, and two Dutch 'police actions' ( 1947, 1948) - UN and US
  • pressure produced the Round Table Conference at The Hague and the transfer of
  • sovereignty on 27 December 1949.
questions.source_exam: V Semester MGU UGP (Honours) - 2024 Admission regular Examination October 2026

questions.question: Give one example of women's participation in an anti-colonial movement. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Sarojini Naidu leading the Dharasana salt satyagraha (May 1930) - Aruna Asaf Ali
  • hoisting the Congress flag at Gowalia T ank, Bombay, on 9 August 1942 - Usha Mehta's

  • commanding the Rani of Jhansi Regiment of the INA (1943) - Akkamma Cherian leading
  • the Travancore State Congress rally (1938) - women couriers and fighters in Kenya's Mau
  • Mau and Algeria's FLN (Djamila Bouhired). [Any one example]

questions.question: What was one major cause of civilian suffering during the Nigerian Civil War? / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• The Federal Military Government's land, sea and air blockade of Biafra (1967-70) cut off
  • food and medical supplies - mass starvation and kwashiorkor, especially among children-
  • starvation used as a weapon of war ('all is fair in war, and starvation is one of the
  • weapons of war') - estimates of deaths range from about 500,000 to 3 million (1 to 2
  • million most often cited), mostly civilians dying of famine - relief reached only through a
  • clandestine church airlift to the Uli airstrip.
questions.source_exam: V Semester MGU UGP (Honours) - 2024 Admission regular Examination October 2026

questions.question: How did colonial rulers use the policy of divide and rule? / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Colonial rulers deliberately fostered and institutionalised differences of religion, caste,
  • ethnicity or region among the colonised (divide et impera) to prevent united resistance- in
  • India: Partition of Bengal (1905), separate electorates for Muslims under the Morley -
  • Minto Reforms (1909), the Communal Award (1932) and 'martial races' recruitment - in
  • Rwanda the Belgians favoured the Tutsi and introduced ethnic identity cards (1933) -
  • indirect rule kept Northern and Southern Nigeria apart - these categories later hardened
  • into postcolonial conflict.
questions.source_exam: V Semester MGU UGP (Honours) - 2024 Admission regular Examination October 2026

questions.question: Why can weak government control over remote or border regions increase the risk of insurgent violence? / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Remote and border regions with rough terrain and thin administrative, police and
  • infrastructural presence offer insurgents safe havens, supply ro utes and recruits - porous
  • borders allow cross -border sanctuary, arms and drug trafficking - neglect and lack of
  • services breed alienation, letting insurgents act as a parallel government - Fearon and
  • Laitin (2003): weak state capacity and rough terrain, rath er than ethnic diversity alone,
  • predict insurgency - e.g., India's Northeast, the 'Red Corridor', the Sahel, Myanmar's
  • borderlands, the Afghanistan-Pakistan frontier.
questions.source_exam: V Semester MGU UGP (Honours) - 2024 Admission regular Examination October 2026

questions.question: What is neo-nationalism? / [CO3] (2024 ADMISSION ONWARDS)
questions.solution_html:
• A renewed form of nationalism, prominent since the end of the Cold War and especially
  • after the 2008 financial crisis - defensive and exclusionary, stressing cultural
  • homogeneity, sovereignty and border control against globalisation, immigration and
  • supranational bodies - often linked to right -wing populism and majoritarianism - e.g.,
  • Brexit (2016), 'America First', anti-immigrant parties in Europe- Eger and Valdez (2015)-
  • the term was earlier used by Tom Nairn, The Break -up of Britain: Crisis and Neo -
  • Nationalism (1977).

questions.question: Why are strong institutions considered essential for successful nation- building? / [CO4]
questions.solution_html:
• Institutions (constitution, independent judiciary, election commission, professional
  • bureaucracy, rule of law) give a new state legitimacy, stability and c ontinuity beyond
  • individual leaders - channel conflict through peaceful, rule -bound means - protect rights
  • and minorities- deliver services and development, building citizens' trust - Acemoglu and
  • Robinson, Why Nations Fail (2012): inclusive institutions sust ain prosperity, extractive
  • ones produce decay- e.g., India's constitutional democracy and Botswana, contrasted with
  • recurrent military coups in Pakistan.
questions.source_exam: V Semester MGU UGP (Honours) - 2024 Admission regular Examination October 2026

questions.question: What is meant by 'citizenship'? / [CO4]
questions.solution_html:
• Citizenship is the legal status of full membership of a political community (the state),
  • carrying rights and duties - T. H. Marshall, Citizenship and Social Class (1950): civil,
  • political and social rights- acquired by birth (jus soli), descent (jus sanguinis), registration
  • or naturalisation- also implies participation and a sense of belonging - in India governed
  • by Part II (Articles 5-11) of the Constitution and the Citizenship Act, 1955.

questions.question: Give one benefit of regional cooperation among postcolonial states. / [CO4] [2x10 = 20]
questions.solution_html:
• Greater collective bargaining power in global forums - expansion of trade and markets
  • (e.g., AfCFTA, SAFTA) - peaceful settlement of disputes and regional security - shared
  • infrastructure, connectivity, disaster management and resource sharing - e.g., ASEAN
  • (Bangkok Declaration, 1967) promoting peace and economic integration in Southeast
  • Asia; also the African Union, SAARC, BIMSTEC. [Any one benefit]

questions.question: Explain Amilcar Cabral's idea of culture as a weapon of struggle. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Amílcar Cabral (1924 -73), founder -leader of the PAIGC (1956), led the liberation
  • struggle of Guinea -Bissau and Cape Verde against Portugal - 'National Liberation and
  • Culture' (Eduardo Mondlane Memorial Lecture, Syracuse University, 1970): imperialism
  • seeks to destroy the culture of the dom inated, because culture is the expression of a
  • people's history - hence 'national liberation is necessarily an act of culture' - culture
  • survived among the rural masses as the basis of resistance - the assimilated petty
  • bourgeoisie must 're -Africanise' and id entify with the masses, 'committing suicide as a
  • class' ('The Weapon of Theory', Havana, 1966)- the idea of a 'return to the source' (Return
  • to the Source , 1973) - culture to be critically renewed, not romanticised: retain positive
  • elements, discard negativ e ones (tribalism, superstition) - in liberated zones the PAIGC
  • built schools, health posts and people's stores, making culture a weapon of struggle -
  • assassinated in Conakry on 20 January 1973; independence declared on 24 September
  • 1973.
questions.source_exam: V Semester MGU UGP (Honours) - 2024 Admission regular Examination October 2026

questions.question: Explain the role of women in the Indian independence movement, with examples. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Early phase: wo men in Swadeshi boycotts (1905) - Bhikaiji Cama unfurled an Indian
  • flag at the International Socialist Congress, Stuttgart (1907) - Annie Besant's Home Rule
  • League (1916) and Congress presidency (1917) - Gandhian mass phase drew women into
  • picketing liquor an d foreign -cloth shops, spinning and khadi - Civil Disobedience:
  • Sarojini Naidu (first Indian woman Congress President, 1925) at Dharasana; Kamaladevi
  • Chattopadhyay; thousands courting arrest - revolutionary nationalism: Pritilata Waddedar
  • (Pahartali raid, 1932), Bina Das, Kalpana Datta- Quit India: Aruna Asaf Ali, Usha Mehta,
  • Sucheta Kripalani, Matangini Hazra (shot at Tamluk, 1942) - Kasturba Gandhi died in
  • detention (1944) - INA's Rani of Jhansi Regiment under Lakshmi Sahgal - Kerala:
  • Akkamma Cherian (1938) - fifteen women in the Constituent Assembly - limits:
  • nationalism often subordinated the 'women's question' (Partha Chatterjee; Geraldine
  • Forbes, Women in Modern India).
questions.source_exam: V Semester MGU UGP (Honours) - 2024 Admission regular Examination October 2026

questions.question: Discuss how national symbols, such as the image of the motherland, often use female imagery. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• The nation is commonly imagined as a mother or goddess to be loved, served and
  • protected- Bharat Mata: Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay's 'Vande Mataram' in
  • Anandamath (1882); Abanindranath Tagore's Bharat Mata (1905) painted during the
  • Swadeshi movement; cartographic images fusing goddess and map (Sumathi
  • Ramaswamy, The Goddess and the Nation, 2010); Bharat Mata Mandir, Varanasi (1936)-
  • elsewhere: Marianne (France), Britannia, Mother Russia, Mother Ireland - Nira Yuval -
  • Davis, Gender and Nation (1997): women as biological and cultural reproducers and
  • symbolic 'border guards' of the nation - national honour located in women's bodies, hence
  • sexual violence against women in conflicts (Partition, 1947) - Anne McClintock: 'all
  • nationalisms are gendered'; women serve as symbols while denied direct political agency-
  • such imagery may also carry a religious idiom that excludes minorities.
questions.source_exam: V Semester MGU UGP (Honours) - 2024 Admission regular Examination October 2026

questions.question: Describe the role of the international community during and after the Rwandan genocide. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Before: UNAMIR (Resolution 872, October 1993) under General Roméo Dallaire -
  • Dallaire's 'genocide fax' (11 January 19 94) warning of planned killings went unheeded -
  • During (7 April to mid -July 1994; about 800,000 Tutsi and moderate Hutu killed,
  • estimates ranging from about 500,000 to over a million): foreign nationals evacuated -
  • after ten Belgian peacekeepers were killed, Belgium withdrew- Resolution 912 (21 April)
  • cut UNAMIR to 270- the US, shadowed by Somalia (1993), avoided the word 'genocide' -
  • Resolution 918 (17 May) imposed an arms embargo, but troops arrived late - France's
  • Opération Turquoise (Resolution 929, June 19 94) was criticised for letting perpetrators
  • escape to Zaire - After: RPF victory (July 1994) - ICTR at Arusha (Resolution 955,
  • November 1994); Akayesu judgment (1998) held that rape can constitute genocide -
  • refugee crisis in Goma and the Congo wars- Clinton's apology (1998), Kofi Annan's 'deep
  • remorse' (1999, Carlsson inquiry), Macron's acknowledgement of responsibility (2021) -
  • gacaca courts- stimulus to the Responsibility to Protect doctrine (2001, 2005).
questions.source_exam: V Semester MGU UGP (Honours) - 2024 Admission regular Examination October 2026

questions.question: Explain how the Berlin Conference of 1884-85 led to the arbitrary division of Africa. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Convened by Bismarck in Berlin (November 1884 to February 1885); fourteen states
  • attended, no African was represented- General Act of Berlin (1885): principle of effective
  • occupation and notification of claims- Leopold II's claim over the Congo recognised; free
  • trade in the Congo basin and free navigatio n of the Congo and Niger - accelerated the
  • Scramble for Africa- the conference set rules; most frontiers were then fixed by bilateral
  • treaties on European maps, using rivers, lines of latitude and longitude and other straight
  • lines- boundaries ignored ethni c, linguistic, ecological and political realities - divided
  • peoples: the Somali (among British, Italian and French Somaliland, Ethiopia and Kenya),
  • the Ewe (Gold Coast and Togoland), the Maasai (Kenya and Tanganyika), the Bakongo -
  • grouped rival societies in to single colonies (Nigeria, Sudan) - the OAU (Cairo, 1964)
  • accepted colonial borders, leaving a legacy of border wars (Ogaden), secessionism
  • (Biafra, Katanga) and irredentism.
questions.source_exam: V Semester MGU UGP (Honours) - 2024 Admission regular Examination October 2026

questions.question: Explain the main sources of economic tension in postcolonial states. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Colonial economic structure: dependence on export of primary commodities,
  • monoculture, weak industrial base - uneven regional development (coast versus interior,
  • East versus West Pakistan leading to the Six -Point Programme and 1971) - control of
  • natural resources and the 'resource curse' (Niger Delta oil) - economic inequality between
  • ethnic groups (Malaysia's 1969 riots and New Economic Policy, 1971; expulsion of
  • Asians from Uganda, 1972) - unresolved land question (Kenya; Zimbabwe's fast -track
  • land reform, 2000) - 1980s debt crisis and IMF -World Bank Structural Adjustment
  • Programmes cutting subsidies and public spending - neo-colonialism (Kwame Nkrumah,
  • 1965) and dependency (Andre Gunder Frank; Walter Rodney, How Europe
  • Underdeveloped Africa, 1972) - unemployment, rural-urban divide and 'sons of the soil'
  • movements- debate between state-led planning and market liberalisation (India, 1991).
questions.source_exam: V Semester MGU UGP (Honours) - 2024 Admission regular Examination October 2026

questions.question: Discuss the aims and achievements of the New Development Bank set up by BRICS. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Agreement signed at the Sixth BRICS Summit, Fortaleza (July 2014); operational from
  • 2015 with headquarters in Shanghai- authorised capital US$100 billion; initial subscribed
  • capital US$50 billion sh ared equally by Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa -
  • equal voting, no veto - aims: mobilise resources for infrastructure and sustainable
  • development in BRICS and other emerging and developing economies; complement and
  • offer an alternative to Western-dominated Bretton Woods institutions; promote lending in
  • local currencies - presidents: K. V. Kamath (India), Marcos Troyjo (Brazil), Dilma
  • Rousseff (since 2023, re -elected 2025) - achievements: about 139 projects and roughly
  • US$43 billion approved by mid -2026 (transport, water, clean energy, urban
  • development); green bonds in China's market (from 2016); COVID -19 emergency
  • lending (up to US$10 billion); membership extended to Bangladesh, the UAE, Egypt,
  • Algeria and Uzbekistan - limitations: small scale rela tive to the World Bank, continuing
  • dollar dependence (local -currency lending about 30 per cent), freezing of new Russian
  • projects after 2022 sanctions.
questions.source_exam: V Semester MGU UGP (Honours) - 2024 Admission regular Examination October 2026

questions.question: Discuss how social media has changed the way nationalist movements organise and communicate. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Social media allows rapid, low -cost, decentralised and often leaderless mobilisation
  • through hashtag s, groups and encrypted messaging - bypasses state -controlled and
  • mainstream media - enables diaspora participation ('long -distance nationalism') - spreads
  • national symbols through memes, images and videos - examples: Arab Spring (2011),
  • #EndSARS (2020), Sri L anka's Aragalaya (2022), Nepal's 'Gen Z' protests (2025) -
  • Zeynep Tufekci, Twitter and Tear Gas (2017): networked movements mobilise quickly
  • but are weak in organisation and negotiation; Manuel Castells, Networks of Outrage and
  • Hope (2012)- darker side: maj oritarian 'digital nationalism', organised troll networks,
  • misinformation, hate speech and echo chambers - states respond with surveillance,
  • censorship and internet shutdowns.
questions.source_exam: V Semester MGU UGP (Honours) - 2024 Admission regular Examination October 2026

questions.question: Discuss the reasons why some postcolonial states retained the coloniser's language as an official language. / [CO4]
questions.solution_html:
• Linguistic diversity: a 'neutral' link language avoided the dominance of one group
  • (Nigeria with over 500 languages; India's Article 343 retained English alongside Hindi;
  • anti-Hindi agitation in Tamil Nadu, 1965; Official Languages Act, 1963) - administration,
  • law, courts and higher education already functioned in that language - the nationalist elite
  • was educated in it - access to science, technology, global trade and diplomacy - national
  • unity and cost of transition - e.g., French in Senegal and Côte d'Ivoire, English in Ghana,
  • Kenya (with Kiswahili) and the Philippines - Rwanda's switc h from French to English
  • (2008) shows strategic choice - critique: Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o, Decolonising the Mind
  • (1986): language carries culture, so its retention prolongs mental colonisation and elitism;
  • Chinua Achebe defended adapting English - contrasts: Kiswahili in Tanzania; Sri Lanka's
  • Sinhala Only Act (1956) fuelled ethnic conflict.
questions.source_exam: V Semester MGU UGP (Honours) - 2024 Admission regular Examination October 2026

questions.question: Explain how citizenship laws can reflect a state's idea of national identity. / [CO4] [5x6 = 30]
questions.solution_html:
• Rules of jus soli (birth) imply a civic, territorial idea of the nation; jus sanguinis
  • (descent) implies an ethnic idea (Rogers Brubaker, 1992, on France and Germany) - India:
  • the Constitution adopted an inclusive, civic jus soli model; amendments of 1986 (one
  • parent to be Indian) and 2003 (neither parent an illegal migrant) moved towards descent
  • (Niraja Gopal Jayal, Citizenship and Its Discontents , 2013) - Citizenship (Amendm ent)
  • Act, 2019 (Rules, March 2024): faster citizenship for Hindu, Sikh, Buddhist, Jain, Parsi
  • and Christian migrants from Afghanistan, Bangladesh and Pakistan who entered before
questions.source_exam: V Semester MGU UGP (Honours) - 2024 Admission regular Examination October 2026

questions.question: Discuss the role of newspapers, books, and other media in building a shared national identity, using Anderson's ideas. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Benedict Anderson, Imagined Communities (1983; revised 1991): the nation is 'an
  • imagined political community, and imagined as both inherently limited and sovereign' -
  • imagined because members never meet most of their fellows, yet hold an image of their
  • communion- a 'deep, horizontal comradeship' - preconditions: decline of sacred script -
  • languages (Latin), dynastic realms and cosmological time, replaced by 'homogeneous,
  • empty time' (Walter Benjam in)- print-capitalism: books as early mass commodities;
  • vernacular print -languages created unified fields of exchange, fixed languages and
  • produced 'languages of power' - the novel and the newspaper represent simultaneity,
  • readers imagining others reading t he same news; the newspaper as a 'one -day best-seller'
  • and its reading as a 'mass ceremony' (Hegel's morning prayer) - Creole pioneers and
  • colonial nationalism: bilingual intelligentsia, schools and administrative 'pilgrimages';
  • census, map and museum shape d the colonial state's imagination (1991 edition) - India:
  • Hicky's Bengal Gazette (1780); Amrita Bazar Patrika (1868); Tilak's Kesari and
  • Mahratta (1881); Vernacular Press Act (1878); novels such as Anandamath; Kerala's
  • Swadeshabhimani, whose editor K. Rama krishna Pillai was banished (1910) - later radio,
  • cinema and social media- critique: Partha Chatterjee ('Whose imagined community?', The
  • Nation and Its Fragments , 1993): if colonial nationalisms only borrowed modular
  • European forms, 'what do they have left to imagine?'; anticolonial nationalism first
  • claimed sovereignty in the spiritual 'inner domain' - low literacy meant oral, performative
  • and religious media mattered too - neglect of gender and religion - conclusion: Anderson
  • explains how media make the nation thinkable, though not every form of national feeling.
questions.source_exam: V Semester MGU UGP (Honours) - 2024 Admission regular Examination October 2026

questions.question: Critically discuss how the legacies of colonial rule have contributed to internal conflict in postcolonial states. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Artificial borders: Berlin Conference (1884 -85), Durand Line (1893), Radcliffe Line
  • (1947) left divided peoples, irredentism and secession (Biafra, Katanga, Eritrea,
  • Kashmir)- colonial classification and census turned fluid identities into rigid categories:
  • Mahmood Mamdani, Citizen and Subject (1996) on 'decentralised despotism' and When
  • Victims Become Killers (2001) on Rwanda's racialised Hutu -Tutsi divide- divide and rule
  • and uneven favour: separate electorates and Partition in India; British reliance on English-
  • educated Tamils in Ceylon followed by the Sinhala Only Act (1956), Black July (1983)
  • and civil war till 2009- separate administration: Sudan's Southern Policy (1930), two civil
  • wars and South Sudan's independence (2011); India's Northeast under the Inner Line and
  • excluded areas- distorted economies and resource enclaves: Niger Delta oil - authoritarian
  • colonial state apparatus inherited: sedition laws, emergency powers, AFSPA (1958)
  • modelled on a 1942 ordinance - settler land alienation: Kenya, Zimbabwe - critical
  • evaluation: colonialism is not the sole cause; postcolonial elites' majoritarian nation -
  • building, centralisation, corruption, Cold War interventions and economic failure also
  • matter (Basil Davidson, The Black Man's Burden, 1992, on the 'curse of the nation-state')-
  • conclusion: colonial legacies created the structures of conflict, while postcolonial choices
  • often activated them.
questions.source_exam: V Semester MGU UGP (Honours) - 2024 Admission regular Examination October 2026

questions.question: Examine the causes and consequences of a major migration crisis of your choice. / [CO4]
questions.solution_html:
• Model answer: the Rohingya crisis - background: Rohingy a Muslims of Rakhine
  • (Arakan) state; colonial -era labour migration from Chittagong and communal violence
  • during the Second World War (1942) shaped later suspicion - Burmese Buddhist
  • nationalism portrays them as illegal 'Bengalis' - causes: Burma Citizenship Law (1982)
  • excluded them from recognised 'national races', making most stateless; restrictions on
  • movement, marriage, education; violence of 2012; anti -Muslim campaigns (969
  • movement, Ma Ba Tha) and hate speech on Facebook; ARSA attacks (25 August 2017)
  • followed by military 'clearance operations' with mass killing, rape and burning of
  • villages- consequences: over 700,000 fled to Bangladesh in 2017; today over one million
  • live in 33 camps at Cox's Bazar (Kutupalong) and on Bhasan Char - strain on Bangladesh:
  • environment, host-community tensions, security, aid cuts - secondary flight by sea and to
  • India, Malaysia and Indonesia - legal action: The Gambia v. Myanmar at the ICJ (2019;
  • provisional measures, January 2020), ICC investigation (2019) and the Prosecutor's
  • warrant request against Senior General Min Aung Hlaing (2024) - the 2021 coup and
  • renewed fighting in Rakhine have blocked safe return - illustrates how exclusionary,
  • ethno-religious nation-building produces statelessness and mass displacement. [Answers
  • on any other major crisis, such as Partition (1947), Bangladesh (1971), the Syrian refugee
  • crisis (since 2011) or Sudan (since 2023), may be valued on the same lines of causes and
  • consequences.]
questions.source_exam: V Semester MGU UGP (Honours) - 2024 Admission regular Examination October 2026

questions.question: Examine how postcolonial diplomacy has changed since the end of the Cold War. / [CO4] [10x2 = 20]
questions.solution_html:
• During the Cold War, postcolonial diplomacy centred on Non -Alignment (Bandung,
  • 1955; Belgrade, 1961) and Third World solidarity (G77, NIEO) - end of bipolarity (1991)
  • reduced NAM's relevance- shift from ideological to pragmatic and economic diplomacy:
  • liberalisation (India, 1991), WTO (1995), trade agreements - India: Look East (1991 -92)
  • to Act East (2014); full relations with Israel (1992); Pokhran -II (1998); Indo -US civil
  • nuclear agreement (2005 -08); 'strategic autonomy' and 'multi -alignment': Quad (revived
  • 2017) alongside SCO (2017) and BRICS - new South -South coali tions: IBSA (2003),
  • BRICS (2009; expanded from 2024), G20 summits (2008), New Development Bank -
  • China's rise and the Belt and Road Initiative (2013); African states balancing China, the
  • West, Russia, Turkey and the Gulf - regionalism: African Union (2002), AfCFTA,
  • ASEAN- new agendas: terrorism after 9/11, climate diplomacy (common but
  • differentiated responsibilities; Paris, 2015; loss and damage fund, 2022), health and
  • vaccine diplomacy, diaspora and soft power - the 'Global South' voice: India's G20
  • presidency (2023) admitting the African Union as a permanent member; Voice of the
  • Global South Summits; India's BRICS chairship (New Delhi summit, 2026) - abstentions
  • on the 2022 Ukraine resolution show hedging - continuing limits: demands for UN
  • Security Council re form, asymmetries of power - conclusion: from collective non -
  • alignment to multi-aligned, interest-based diplomacy in a multipolar world.
questions.source_exam: V Semester MGU UGP (Honours) - 2024 Admission regular Examination October 2026
